newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AUSI said frontrunner in Australia iron race.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AUSI said frontrunner in Australia iron race.

text.p: Australian United Steel Industry Ltd (AUSI), led by former CRA Ltd heads Sir Russel Madigan and Sir Roderick Carnegie, is at an advanced stage of arranging billions of dollars finance for its direct reduced iron (DRI) plant in Western Australia and is front-runner in a field of competing projects, Madigan said on Thursday.
Construction was expected to begin by the first half of next year, if not before, Madigan he said in an interview.
"Absolutely. I think we are the front-runner," Madigan said.
"It's purely a matter of finance for us. We've been very low profile, unlike some people," he said.
A meeting of the privately-held company's board to be held on Friday was expected to mark further progress. Arrangement of finance was on track, he said.
Madigan would not reveal details of how much the Cape Lambert plant will cost.
But at 3.6 million tonnes a year, the biggest in the world, the cost would run to several billions of dollars.

A go-ahead for the AUSI project would make it the second into processed iron production in Western Australia, behind the Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd (BHP), with its A$1.5 billion Port Hedland hot briquetted iron (HBI) plant.
AUSI and competing plants are springing up to feed massive growth in electric arc furnace (EAF) steelmaking in East Asia.

East Asian countries plan to bring an extra 83.2 million tonnes of steelmaking capacity on stream between 1996 and early next decade, a study released this week by the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) shows.
EAF plants, in Indonesia, South Korea, Thailand, Singapore, China, the Philippines, Malaysia, Vietnam and Taiwan involve additional capacity of 40.5 million tonnes.
ABARE, Australia's official commodities forecasting agency, said annual world EAF steel production was projected to increase by 90 million tonnes to 330 million tonnes in year 2005.
Annual EAF production in East Asia, excluding Japan, was projected to increase by 33 million tonnes to 85 million tonnes in year 2005, an increase of nearly 60 percent.

With Asia's plans for new steel capacity split between conventional integrated steelmaking plants and EAF, Asia's new steel projects offer Australia significant export opportunities through the supply of processed iron through major new processing projects, the ABARE study said.

In projects spread through Taiwan, China, Thailand, Malaysia, South Korea, Indonesia and the Philippines, new conventional integrated steel plants in East Asia involve additional capacity of 42.7 million tonnes of steel.

Nine proposed plants in Western Australia are now competing to produce DRI or other forms of processed iron ore, the ABARE study shows. These include Asia Iron Ltd's 1.5 million tonne HBI plant; AUSI's 3.6 million tonnes DRI plant; BHP's A$1.5 billion 2.0-2.5 million tonne HBI plant (to commence full production mid-1988); Compact Steel Ltd's 2.0 million tonne HBI plant and its 1.4 million tonne steel coil plant.

They also include: Hamersley Iron's 2.0 million tonne HBI plant, Kingstream Resources NL's A$1.4 billion 2.0 million tonne DRI plant and its 2.4 million tonne steel slab plant; Mineralogy Pty Ltd's 4.0 million tonne
HBI plant and its 3.0 million steel coil plant; Mitsubishi Corp's 400,000-500,000 tonne iron carbide plant; and Robe River Mining Ltd's 5 million tonne pellet plant.
"The eventual number (of listed projects) which are completed will be a function of market factors," ABARE said.
Assuming an average selling price of A$190 a tonne, ABARE estimates BHP's plant would generate annual export revenue of about A$400 million.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
